name: Brute Force Login — Multiple Failed Authentication Attempts
description: Multiple failed login attempts from the same source IP within a short time window, exceeding the threshold for normal authentication failures.
false_positives: Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Rapid7)
Authentication testing tools used by red team
Misconfigured service accounts with cached wrong password
Password manager failures after a recent password change

name: Suspicious PowerShell Execution — Encoded Command
description: PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand or execution policy bypass flags from an unusual parent process, indicating potential malware payload execution.
false_positives: Authorized administrative scripts run by IT operations
Software deployment tools (SCCM, Ansible, Puppet)
Legitimate security tools that use encoded PowerShell
Developer workflows using encoded commands for special character handling

name: Malicious Office Child Process — Macro Execution Indicator
description: Office application (Word, Excel, Outlook) spawned a shell process (cmd, powershell, wscript). This is a high-fidelity indicator of a malicious macro executing a payload. This is NOT process injection (T1055) — it is user execution of a malicious file (T1204.002). Process injection requires evidence of code written into another process's memory space.
false_positives: Legitimate Office macros used for business automation (confirm with document owner)
IT-deployed macros via Group Policy for legitimate workflows
Office automation via COM objects used by authorized applications

name: Network Port Scan — Reconnaissance Activity
description: Single source IP sending SYN packets to more than 50 unique destination ports — consistent with automated port scanning (Nmap, Masscan) for network reconnaissance.
matched_conditions_template: Suricata signature: ET SCAN (SYN Scan Detected)
{count} unique port probes observed from attacker
false_positives: Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Rapid7 InsightVM)
Network monitoring tools performing port checks (Zabbix, Nagios)
Internal red team or authorized penetration testing activity
Load balancer health checks generating connection patterns

name: Access Token Manipulation — Sensitive Privileges Assigned
description: Sensitive privileges (SeDebugPrivilege, SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeTcbPrivilege) were assigned to a non-service logon session, followed by privileged service access. This indicates access token manipulation. NOTE: Event 4672 alone does not prove privilege escalation — it proves token privileges exist. Correlation with LSASS access (Sysmon 10) strengthens this. T1134 is correct here, NOT T1548 (which requires UAC bypass or setuid evidence).
matched_conditions_template: Event ID = 4672 (Special Privileges Assigned to New Logon)
false_positives: Legitimate administrative tools (Process Explorer, WinDbg) that require SeDebugPrivilege
Security software (EDR agents, antivirus) with elevated token access
IT automation tools running under service accounts with elevated privileges
Database services requiring SeImpersonatePrivilege (SQL Server, IIS)

name: Persistence via Registry Run Key Modification
description: A new entry was written to HKLM or HKCU CurrentVersion\Run registry key by a non-installer process. This is a common persistence mechanism used by malware to survive reboots. High confidence when cmd.exe or powershell.exe writes the key rather than a legitimate installer (msiexec.exe, setup.exe).
matched_conditions_template: Written by process: {process_name} (expected: msiexec.exe or installer)
false_positives: Legitimate software installers that add themselves to startup (verify with IT asset inventory)
IT-deployed software using run keys for agent persistence (AV, EDR, monitoring agents)
User-installed applications that autostart (messaging apps, cloud sync tools)
